P1.evidence: Setter notes were read back specifically and landed well — 'Kim told me a little bit about you. So, you're in field sales, so to speak. You've been, you're driving, driving all day. You have a six-year-old sun.' plus 'you've already been doing some Trevor's morning routines'. No four-part frame was set and no frame agreement was sought. The opening question was a state check rather than the scripted open — 'how are you actually feeling into today's call?' — followed by 'walk me through where things are right now in terms of training. Honestly, the good weeks, the bad weeks, everything', which is a good but narrower substitute.

P2.evidence: The most complete baseline in the batch. Height was asked directly ('and how tall are you?'), weight and age confirmed ('Imagine your son is 6, you're 38?'). Work was covered properly including whether it is desk-bound — established as long driving plus sitting. Injuries and chronic pain were pursued to duration and impact: 'how long has that actually been going on?' / 'Like two years' / 'And how is that affecting your day-to-day?'. Training week, results and diet were all covered. Two gaps: general and hereditary health conditions were never asked as a category — only the specific back pain the setter had flagged was pursued — and sleep was volunteered unprompted ('I had bad quality sleep') without ever being asked, which the spec scores as a miss. Daily energy was never asked.

P3.evidence: Reached the right destination but the rep supplied much of the emotional content instead of asking for it. The surface goals were drawn out cleanly — 'what kind of results do you actually want to see?' — and the close-out reflection was strong: 'the version 2.0 of Jan... the guy who is pain-free, who's strong, who can match whatever his son throws at him in the next 10-20 years'. But the bridge to the deeper why was rep-led: rather than asking what is driving this, he asserted the second thing himself ('one thing is showing up for your work and not being in pain. But second thing, like your son is six, right?') and then supplied the ten-year projection. The 'when you're moving better, what does that actually do for you' question was never asked, and 'who else does that impact' was answered by the rep rather than the prospect. The script credits asking; here the prospect largely agreed with conclusions handed to him.

P4.evidence: Ran well and produced the key admission. The rep pushed past the first answer — 'Okay, but like, why is that? Why are sometimes you working out, sometimes not?' — and kept going until Jan named the gap himself: 'the structure, I think I'm lacking I'm a lot, Definitely.' The history of failed attempts, including physiotherapy and self-directed YouTube programming, was fully surfaced. P4f is partial because the rep asserted the conclusion rather than asking the question — 'it's not like a discipline problem because it's a structural problem, yeah?' — which got agreement but not self-discovery.

P5.evidence: A consequence frame was run and it did real work, which is the main thing separating this call from the Mike Chenard call the same day. The future-cost question was asked twice — 'if you don't take care of this, you don't address this, like, what is it going to be like in one[year]?' producing 'It's going to be worse', and later 'ask yourself this if you won't commit now, how much it will cost you in the future?' which produced the prospect's own strongest line: 'if I'm going to be doing what I've done until now, I'm going to be getting what I got.' The line-in-the-sand move was delivered too, though as a statement rather than a question — 'you need to draw the line in the sand and actually commit to it'. The willing-to-settle and why-not pair was never run, so the frame was asserted rather than extracted.

P6.evidence: The cleanest commitment check in the batch and it was completed before any price was mentioned. The belief question ran in full — 'If you had those three things dialed in, do you think you would get where you want to be? Stronger, pain-free?' — and produced an honest, useful answer ('It is scary'), which the rep then worked rather than skipped. The all-in question was asked directly and answered: 'if we can figure out the details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work to become the dad you just described?' / 'I want to. Yes.' Only then did he move to logistics. The isolate was also re-run after price landed: 'let's put finances aside for a second. Apart from that, is there anything else, any other reason that will stop you from being 100% in on this?'

P11.evidence: Executed nearly in full and the best P11 in this batch. Payment was collected live and confirmed — 'All right, processing' / 'Okay, got you, man.' The onboarding call with Trevor was booked on the call for the following evening at 7.15 and verified in the prospect's calendar. The agreement email was confirmed to have arrived and was signed on the call — 'You were invited to review and sign a document' then 'All right. I've signed that.' Step 4 is partial: the rep named the app, the Skool community and the onboarding form as things signing unlocks — 'you're going to get the access to the app, where everything is held, to the school community, and the onboarding call to fill out' — but never instructed him to read the welcome email or complete the questionnaire before the Trevor call.

objection_plays.detail: The isolate ran textbook — 'let's put finances aside for a second. Apart from that, is there anything else, any other reason that will stop you from being 100% in on this? Or is it just pure financial question?' — and produced a clean 'it's just the financials, nothing more'. The break-it-up move ran when the card limit surfaced. Everything else was skipped: no should-I-versus-how reframe, no permission question for the money conversation, and none of the financial picture — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no count of cards, no available credit, no investments. The only figure sought was the card limit, which the prospect could not find. In practice the prospect did the persuasion himself, comparing the price to a trip to Africa and to back surgery; the rep mostly stayed out of the way, which worked here but is not the play.

The trigger was explicit and unprompted — 'i don't want to really like say straightforward that i need to talk to my wife but i do'. Not one of the six scripted moves was run. The rep did not ask whether, money aside, he personally believed it could get him there in the context of his wife; did not ask what obstacles might come up in that conversation; did not ask whether there was any reason she would not want him stronger and out of pain; did not test permission-versus-input; did not use the not-a-joint-decision frame; and did not offer the deposit-with-refund fallback. He did not acknowledge the statement at all, redirected to isolating finances, and took payment 23 minutes later. This is the single largest process failure on an otherwise well-run call, and it is also logged as a conduct flag.

Triggered as a request to defer — 'is there any way how I could go through this and give you guys feedback tomorrow? Or you just need to know it right away now?' The rep declined the delay and surfaced the real blocker, which is the spirit of the play: 'if it's not about the money, is it maybe something doubting yourself that you will actually follow through?' produced a genuine admission about fear of failing. But the scripted moves were absent — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here', no identity move, no closing 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. He finished with an assumptive close instead: 'From what I'm hearing, you already made the decision. You just need someone to, like, pat you on the back.'

Fear was raised repeatedly and honestly — 'It is scary', 'I can definitely say I'm scared uh to to commit', 'you are afraid of failing'. The rep played a fear response and it landed, but none of it was the scripted play: he used 'being scared, that means that you care', the Andy Frisella line 'tell me one thing in your life that is great, that came as a result of being comfortable', and a brain-wired-for-comfort frame. None of the certainty question, the pleasure-versus-pain question, the bridge, the plane analogy or the burned-before analogy were used. Effective improvisation rather than the play as written.

Script gap and the most important one in this call: there is no play, and no stop, for a prospect who discloses a diagnosed structural spinal condition. Jan volunteered an MRI showing a vertebra 'sliding' dorsally and a doctor's assessment that it is not surgical. The playbook offers the rep nothing here — no clearance question, no clinician-contact step, no disqualification path — so he improvised a mechanistic explanation and a therapeutic promise instead. This is the same hole already logged against the Tyron Giuliani call, but inverted: there it lost a qualified prospect, here it closed one who arguably should have been paused pending clearance.

Script gap: payment mechanics as a blocker rather than affordability. The prospect was willing and able to pay but his card limit could not carry a single $6,000 transaction. There is no scripted handling for this; the rep improvised correctly by falling back to the sanctioned two-pay, but only after several minutes of dead air while the prospect searched online banking and fetched his card from his vehicle. Worth a scripted path given how much of this corpus is non-US.

notes: Process-wise the strongest call in the batch and it closed: complete baseline, root cause named by the prospect, a real consequence frame, a commitment check completed before price, and near-perfect payment and onboarding execution. Two things undo that. First, the wife objection was stated plainly and never acknowledged — coach this as a hard stop, because closing through an unaddressed spouse consult is where refunds and chargebacks come from. Second, and more serious than anything in the adherence model, the rep responded to a disclosed MRI-confirmed spinal condition by diagnosing it himself and dismissing the prospect's physio and chiropractor; that is not a rep failure so much as a missing gate in the process, and it should be a mandatory clearance step rather than a coaching point.
